controlled_change: One offline SLRU versus CLOCK policy at identical aligned bytes and demand order over 256 normal generation steps, 128 new input tokens and 32 subsequent generation steps.
correctness: Complete 290-forward, 13,920-layer trace; exact 328-token state reuse, pending output ingestion and unchanged session/memory. First 33 output tokens and 1,584 layer routes reproduce the prior capture. 159 Python tests pass; no new independent logit or coding-quality qualification.
decision_origin: authored interpretation; original report statuses retained
expected_effect: The extended fixed-order simulation suggests 4.95 percent fewer expert reads overall; a smaller native latency benefit is possible but unmeasured.
hypothesis: A 75-percent-protected SLRU cache may reduce normal coding-session latency at the observed 1,848-slot allocation.
limitations: Retrospective interpretation of one instrumented short-history conversation; not a preregistered or paired latency result.
The 4K-history append, 2K/4K/7K acceptance, coding quality and sustained session remain unqualified.
Simulation omits native hit-first admission, live GPU users, OS caching, read overlap and memory compression cost.
The post-append decode regression prevents claiming a uniform cache benefit; no production default is promoted.
outcome: Capture completed in 166.94 seconds. SLRU simulated 5.72 percent fewer first-request decode reads, 9.46 percent fewer append reads and 0.42 percent more subsequent decode reads. Native traced generation was 2.47 tokens/s and append TTFT 24.13 seconds. System swap usage did not grow at recorded boundaries.
smallest_experiment: Implement only this SLRU policy behind an experimental option; verify lifetimes and exact state, then compare short normal requests and follow-ups in alternating pairs at equal admitted memory. Retain CLOCK unless complete-request latency improves.
